sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has played a central role in improving the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and ushering in an “age of LLM agents.” A natural intuition is that LLMs can learn from reward signals by favoring better responses over worse ones. Yet Shao et al. (2026) recently reported that even spurious (random) rewards can improve model performance. Why can a model improve when its rewards are assigned at random, providing no more correctness information than a random coin toss? This counterintuitive finding prompted a number of investigations and led Yan et al. (2026) to coin the term spurious-reward paradox . Explaining it requires understanding what shapes the model’s response to training beyond correctness feedback. There are currently two main lines of explanation for the paradox, but neither provides a complete account in light of our new empirical results. The first attributes the gains to data contamination ( Yan et al., 2026 ) . The gains we observe on synthetically generated problems suggest, however, that the phenomenon cannot be attributed entirely to data leakage. The second looks to particular mechanisms within RL training. Shao et al. (2026) conjecture that clipping in GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) favors behavior to which the model already assigns high probability. Chen et al. (2025) , however, argue that clipping bias does not explain the gains. They explain the paradox through the model’s current performance, as reflected in its rollouts: more accurate models generate fewer incorrect responses that can be rewarded by chance. Nevertheless, when two checkpoints are trained offline on the same rollouts with the same random rewards, the later, higher-accuracy checkpoint shows larger mean gains under both rollout sources. This suggests that understanding the gains requires looking beyond the model’s current performance to properties of the learner that shape its response to the same training signal. In particular, capabilities the model already has but does not fully put to use, or its dormant capability , may play an important role. We instead consider the model’s dormant capability together with the information provided in the question prompt. A model may not yet reliably generate the correct answer, yet the prompt can still elicit behavior that training can act on. Under random rewards, some useful responses may be reinforced by chance; which behaviors can be elicited and reinforced should therefore depend in part on the starting model and the information in the input. On this account, training can improve performance even when the reward does not tell the model which answers are correct. We can therefore use a model’s response to random-reward RL training as a probe. We introduce reachability to describe how far, and how readily, a model can improve from its current state under specified constraints on the training procedure, the information supplied, and the training budget. Specifically, we use random-reward reachability to probe dormant capability. We prove that, under random-reward RL training, the reward channel carries no correctness information, allowing us to study what training can attain without correctness feedback. This isolates the label-leakage side of a longstanding question in probing: whether a successful probe reveals the model’s dormant capability or learns the task from its own supervision ( Hewitt and Liang, 2019 ) . Applying random-reward probing in the wild across OLMo checkpoints reveals three stages of LLM capability development. Early in pre-training, OLMo-2-1124-7B is dormant : even RL with ground-truth (GT) rewards yields little improvement. As pre-training progresses, the model becomes receptive : GT rewards become effective, suggesting that the model has acquired the basic task knowledge needed to benefit from further training. Random rewards remain weak, however, suggesting that the model has acquired relevant knowledge and skills but has yet to integrate them into capabilities it can readily draw on. When the model enters mid-training, it becomes autodidactic : training can now help it put this knowledge to use even without a reward signal that tells it which answers are correct. These results suggest that a model’s receptiveness to post-training depends on its overall capability at that point in training, and that reachability provides a viable way to study it.

sections.heading: Contributions
sections.text: We make three contributions: (1) we provide an alternative account of the spurious-reward paradox that incorporates the starting model and the information in the input (§ 3 ); (2) we formalize reachability as a framework for probing what further training can attain and develop random-reward RL as a correctness-free probe (§ 4 ); and (3) we identify a three-stage pattern in training response that reveals changes not fully reflected in current task performance (§ 5 ).

sections.heading: 2 Background, Related Work, and Experimental Setup
sections.text: Before discussing our experiments and results, we review RL, the spurious-reward paradox, and its two prevailing accounts and their limitations. We then revisit the probing debate: whether a probe reveals the model’s knowledge or learns the task itself. 1 1 1 For the sake of space, we defer a more comprehensive literature review to Appendix 8 .

sections.heading: Reinforcement Learning with Spurious Rewards
sections.text: In a typical RLVR setting 2 2 2 Appendix 7 reviews core RL concepts and notation, following Shao et al. (2026) and Chen et al. (2025) . , the model generates a response, and a verifier assigns a reward by checking the answer or executing tests. Methods such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) can train models without worked solutions by sampling multiple responses to the same prompt and updating the model based on their relative rewards. Surprisingly, Shao et al. (2026) found that even spurious rewards —rewards with little, no, or even negative correlation with answer correctness—can elicit strong reasoning performance under certain conditions. Subsequent work has proposed several explanations for this phenomenon, including reduced reward-misalignment damage in more accurate models ( Chen et al., 2025 ) and increased model confidence through entropy minimization ( Agarwal et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) . In this work, we study spurious rewards from a different perspective. We show that random rewards—a special case of spurious rewards with zero correlation with correctness—can serve as an effective probe of dormant LLM capabilities in generation tasks such as reasoning and coding.

sections.heading: The Probing Debate: Measuring an LLM’s Dormant Capability
sections.text: Probing has long been a central tool for studying what models know and what they are capable of. The usual recipe is straightforward: freeze the model, extract its representations, and train a classifier, or probe , to predict a property of interest. Good probing performance is then taken as evidence that the model has learned something about that property. But whose knowledge have we found? The probe has, after all, been given the answers during training. As Hewitt and Liang (2019) ask, “can we conclude that the representation encodes linguistic structure, or has the probe just learned the task?” This question has motivated different accounts of decodability : what can be recovered from a representation, and under what conditions. Pimentel et al. (2020) formulate probing as estimating mutual information between representations and task labels. But information can be preserved without being easy to extract. The Bayesian account of Pimentel and Cotterell (2021) considers what a learner can extract given its prior knowledge and finite training data. Predictive 𝒱 \mathcal{V} -information makes the predictor family explicit ( Xu et al., 2019 ) , while conditional probing asks what the representation contributes beyond a baseline ( Hewitt et al., 2021 ) . The question thus becomes not merely whether information is present, but under what conditions it can be used. Nevertheless, probes for LLM capabilities still largely rely on supervised learning from task labels and therefore do not remove the concern raised by Hewitt and Liang (2019) : the probe may learn the task from its own supervision. We show that random-reward RL can probe what training can attain while excluding correctness information from the reward signal, thereby isolating this label-leakage component of the broader probing problem. While this debate may seem to have gone quiet, its central questions have only become more relevant and important, resurfacing under different names. Recent work such as sparse autoencoders (SAE; Bricken et al., 2023 , inter alia ) , the linear representation hypothesis ( Park et al., 2023 ; Lampinen et al., 2026 , inter alia ) , and the J-space ( Gurnee et al., 2026 ) again raises the question of what the structures recovered from a model’s representations tell us about what the model knows and can do.

sections.heading: 3 Explaining the Spurious-Reward Paradox: Learner and Input
sections.text: We now examine why LLMs can improve under random-reward RL. Previous accounts ( Shao et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) do not account for two observations we present below: different learner checkpoints respond differently to identical rollouts and rewards, and the same checkpoint responds differently across the two random-token input conditions. These results point to the starting model and the information in the input as additional determinants of training response. Our main experiments follow the publicly released checkpoints of OLMo-2-1124-7B ( OLMo et al., 2025 ) through pre-training (P1) and mid-training (P2). P1 uses a broad corpus dominated by web data, while P2 introduces a curated mixture of high-quality and task-focused data. The checkpoints span both stages, with architecture and parameter count held fixed. We also examine training checkpoints of SmolLM2-1.7B and OLMo-3-7B . 3 3 3 See the checkpoint coverage in Appendix 10.1 and additional checkpoint comparisons in Appendix 11.3 . sections.heading: Different Models Yield Different Learning Outcomes from the Same Rollouts
sections.text: First, we present an offline random-reward RL experiment in which two learner checkpoints are trained on exactly the same rollouts and rewards. We take two OLMo-2-1124-7B checkpoints, one from the end of pre-training (P1: 3,896B tokens) and the first checkpoint in mid-training (P2: +5B tokens). We generate rollouts from each frozen checkpoint and train both learners on each set, giving four source–learner combinations. Within each source, both learners receive exactly the same cached rollouts and random rewards and start from identical LoRA weights. We run 16 paired replicates for 500 updates each. The rollouts remain fixed throughout training, so differences between the learners cannot be attributed to differences in the responses or rewards they receive. The responses generated by P1 can take P2 from 13.5% to 80.0%, while P1 itself reaches at most 9.5% at the endpoint (Table 1 ). With P2 rollouts, the highest terminal scores are 57.0% for P2 and 14.0% for P1. Thus, under either shared rollout source, P2 shows the larger upward changes. Its mean gains are also larger: 4.5 versus 0.6 percentage points with P1 rollouts, and 13.7 versus 2.9 percentage points with P2 rollouts. Recall that Chen et al. (2025) explain the spurious-reward paradox through the model’s current performance and rollout quality, arguing that training stronger models “incurs less total misalignment damage … and is therefore more likely to yield improvements under random rewards.” That mechanism cannot by itself explain the learner difference here: within each source condition, P1 and P2 receive the same responses and the same random rewards, so the number and identity of accidentally rewarded responses are fixed. Their account may still explain variation across rollout sources, but the contrast between learners requires an additional property of the learner itself.

sections.heading: Reachability and an Account of the Spurious-Reward Paradox
sections.text: Taken together, these findings motivate an account of the spurious-reward paradox in terms of the starting model, the information in the input, and the model’s reachability , which we formalize in the next section. In short, the reward function determines how sampled answers are reinforced or suppressed, but the effect of those updates also depends on the starting model and the input. Even when rewards are assigned by random coin tosses and contain no correctness information, the prompt can still elicit useful behavior, and some random updates can reinforce it. If the starting model can already produce task-relevant behavior from the information in the input, some random-reward trajectories may therefore make that behavior more usable and improve task performance. The two experiments examine two factors not captured by rollout quality alone. First, P2 changes more than P1 when trained on identical rollouts and random rewards, showing that the learner state matters. In the second, the two random-token input conditions produce sharply different outcomes. The retained instruction and template markers still specify the task domain, request a reasoning chain, define the final-answer format, and structure the prompt. They do not supply the missing mathematical problem or its answer, but they provide task information that the model can draw on. This gives a different view of dormant capability: random-reward training lets us ask how much task performance further training can attain from a model without correctness feedback through the reward. We call this property reachability .

sections.heading: 4 Reachability Probing with Random-Reward RL
sections.text: This new way of studying a model’s capability offers a general-purpose approach to probing that provides no correctness feedback during adaptation. It thus directly addresses the longstanding question of whether a probe reveals the model’s capability or learns the task from its own supervision. This probe also yields new findings about the development of models’ dormant capability, which are particularly relevant today, when post-training plays an ever more important role in developing LLM capabilities. In this section, we provide a formal definition of our reachability probe. We first discuss what information means when studying a model’s dormant capability, and then formalize reachability. We next present a short proof that random reward signals do not introduce correctness information through the reward channel. Finally, we introduce random-reward RL as a reachability probe, which we use in the next section on real LLMs.

sections.heading: What Do We Mean by Information and Dormant Capability?
sections.text: To study a model’s dormant capability, we need to distinguish the information available to it from its ability to use that information. The question is whether the model has the computational ability to extract the answer. This is what we mean by computational accessibility . Learned lossless compression shows the same distinction: the information in the data is fixed, yet the number of bits needed depends on how well a predictor can model it ( Mao et al., 2022b ; Mao et al., 2023 ) , and text generated by one LLM is highly predictable under another ( Mao et al., 2025c ) . sections.heading: Reachability
sections.text: We introduce reachability to describe how far, and how readily, a model can improve from its current state under specified constraints on the training procedure, the information supplied, and the training budget. These constraints are part of the measurement: the same checkpoint may respond differently when the available supervision or the allowed updates change. Fix an initial checkpoint θ 0 \theta_{0} , a task performance measure J J , and a training budget B B . Let 𝔄 \mathfrak{A} be a prespecified family of adaptation procedures, with constraints on inputs, supervision, parameter updates, selection, and stopping. Writing 𝒜 B ​ ( θ 0 , U ) \mathcal{A}_{B}(\theta_{0};U) for the checkpoint obtained by 𝒜 \mathcal{A} within budget B B under training randomness U U , we define: Reach B ⁡ ( θ 0 ) := sup 𝒜 ∈ 𝔄 𝔼 U ​ [ J ⁡ ( 𝒜 B ​ ( θ 0 , U ) ) ] . \operatorname{Reach}_{B}(\theta_{0}):=\sup_{\mathcal{A}\in\mathfrak{A}}\mathbb{E}_{U}\!\left[J\!\left(\mathcal{A}_{B}(\theta_{0};U)\right)\right]. (3) In words, this is the highest expected task performance attainable from the checkpoint within the given budget using the allowed procedures. Its improvement over current performance is Δ reach ​ ( θ 0 ) := Reach B ⁡ ( θ 0 ) − J ⁡ ( θ 0 ) . \Delta_{\mathrm{reach}}(\theta_{0}):=\operatorname{Reach}_{B}(\theta_{0})-J(\theta_{0}). (4) Both quantities depend on the task, intervention family, and budget; we leave the first two implicit in the notation. The dependence on B B describes the training needed for a given expected performance. Comparing checkpoints under the same constraints can reveal differences in training potential, even when their current scores are similar.

sections.heading: No Correctness Information through Random Rewards
sections.text: The information supplied during training matters when interpreting reachability as a probe of dormant capability. If the training signal identifies correct responses, it can teach the model how to solve the task. Random rewards let us remove this source of supervision. Let X t X_{t} be a training input, A t A_{t} a sampled response, and C t = v ⁡ ( X t , A t ) C_{t}=v(X_{t},A_{t}) its correctness under a verifier v v . Let H t H_{t} denote the preceding training history. Theorem 4.1 (No correctness information through the reward channel) . Suppose each reward R t ∼ Bernoulli ⁡ ( p ) R_{t}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) is sampled independently of the input, response, and preceding training history. Then I ( R t ; C t ∣ H t , X t ) = 0 . I(R_{t};C_{t}\mid H_{t},X_{t})=0. (5) If the initial checkpoint, adaptation protocol, and joint law of its random draws are held fixed, and all training decisions are independent of the verifier, replacing v v with any other verifier leaves the distribution of the training trajectory unchanged. The proof couples the runs under different verifiers using the same random draws. Their inputs, responses, rewards, and updates agree at every step because none uses the verifier; the full argument appears in Appendix 9 . Any performance gain under this protocol therefore occurs without the reward oracle telling the model which responses are correct. Correct answers are used for evaluation only. The model can still learn to use the task information in its inputs more effectively.

sections.text: For probing without correctness feedback, we restrict the allowed procedures to a family 𝔄 0 \mathfrak{A}_{0} whose training signals, selection decisions, and stopping rules satisfy the verifier independence above. In what follows, Reach B \operatorname{Reach}_{B} and Δ reach \Delta_{\mathrm{reach}} refer to this family. This gives us a concrete measure of how much the starting model can benefit from the specified training without requiring us to optimize over every allowed procedure. We use this correctness-free probe in the next section to examine how training response changes across checkpoints.

sections.heading: Dormant, Receptive, and Autodidactic — Three Stages of Training Response Revealed by Reachability Probing
sections.text: Figure 5 illustrates three stages of training response under our reachability probe. Early in pre-training (P1: 34B), the checkpoint is dormant : it shows little performance improvement under either reward signal on synthetic GSM (mean gains of 0.4 and 0.5 percentage points under GT and Random rewards). Later in pre-training (P1: 3,896B), it is receptive : GT rewards produce large gains (a mean gain of 79.5 points from a 2.5% start, with runs ending at 61.5–90.5%), while random-reward RL remains weak (a mean gain of 4.3 points). After the model enters mid-training (P2: +5B), it is autodidactic 4 4 4 Autodidactic means “Self-taught.” Here, we mean improvement without correctness feedback from rewards. : random rewards now yield a mean gain of 26.8 points from a 13.5% start, driven by four of eight runs that reach 59.0–77.5%. This response is not stable across mid-training: over the twelve P2 checkpoints, the mean Random gain ranges from − - 11.8 to +26.8 points and exceeds 10 points at three of them (+5B, +21B, and +42B; Appendix 11.1 ). Figure 6(a) presents the full checkpoint scan, where we observe the same three-stage pattern. Early checkpoints show little improvement under either reward signal; correct rewards become effective as pre-training progresses, followed by the abrupt development of large gains under random rewards in mid-training. A similar ordering appears under supervised fine-tuning (SFT): full SFT becomes effective earlier, whereas number-masked SFT shows its strongest response later (Figure 6(b) ). Interestingly, OLMo-2 exhibits these regimes in sequence as training progresses, with relatively distinct transitions; a similar developmental pattern also appears under SFT. Do these transitions constitute “emergence”? Both the notion of “emergence” itself and whether transitions such as these constitute emergence remain debated ( Wei et al., 2022 ; Schaeffer et al., 2023 ; Niu et al., 2025a , inter alia ) . The agreement between theory and observation nevertheless suggests that capability development follows regularities we have yet to understand. Identifying them could help explain why capabilities develop when they do and what training conditions make that possible.

sections.heading: Similar Patterns across Tasks and Models
sections.text: We observe similar developmental patterns beyond OLMo-2 and arithmetic. On code generation and compositional lookup, random rewards again produce larger gains at later checkpoints (Figure 7 ). The timing is idiosyncratic to each task, however: at 462B tokens, GT training already brings OLMo-2 to 97.5% on lookup but only 8.5% on GSM. Differences in timing also appear across models. In OLMo-3-7B , correct rewards become effective before random rewards, with large random-reward gains appearing later in mid-training than in OLMo-2. Within the checkpoints tested, SmolLM2-1.7B reaches only the receptive stage: correct rewards yield substantial gains while random rewards remain weak. sections.heading: 6 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text: We offer a new explanation for the counterintuitive spurious-reward paradox and find that random-reward RL can be used as a way to probe the development process of an LLM under different training regimes. We believe we have taken a step forward toward a better understanding of LLMs and how their capabilities develop; nevertheless, more questions arise as we edge toward the truth. Our theoretical account and empirical results suggest that there is usable information in input questions that LLMs can use even without correctness feedback from rewards. Nevertheless, studying the exact mechanism by which this information is utilized is a natural extension of this work. It could be a sign that, after a period of training, LLMs begin to bring their knowledge and skills together and show early signs of self-improvement: telling the model what task to attempt may be enough for it to improve through further training. The mechanism could also be superficial. The model may simply learn a better decoding strategy that generates correct responses more reliably. While shallow, such a strategy is certainly a capability; it does not, however, by itself establish the consistency across equivalent expressions that we would expect of “knowledge” ( Niu et al., 2024 ) . Future work can build on these findings by studying how random-reward training affects pass@ k k across sampling budgets ( Yue et al., 2025 ) and the consistency of responses across equivalent questions. Moreover, to keep this paper within a reasonable scope, we focus on RL as the vehicle for reachability-based probing. Yet other modes of post-training can also be used to develop a whole suite of reachability probes that help us better understand LLMs.

sections.heading: 7 Preliminaries: RLVR, GRPO, and Random Rewards
sections.text: RL training generates responses, assigns rewards, and updates the model to favor responses receiving higher rewards. Random-reward training follows the same procedure, except that the reward no longer indicates whether a response is correct. This section introduces the notation used to describe that procedure, following Shao et al. (2024) ; Shao et al. (2026) ; Chen et al. (2025) .

sections.heading: 7.2 Verifiable and Random Rewards
sections.text: In RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR), a task-specific checker supplies the reward. Let V ⁡ ( x , y ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } V(x,y)\in\{0,1\} indicate whether response y y answers question x x correctly. Our ground-truth (GT) condition uses r ⁡ ( x , y ) = V ⁡ ( x , y ) r(x,y)=V(x,y) . On arithmetic, the checker evaluates the extracted final answer, so different solutions can receive the same reward. On code, it executes the generated program against tests. The Random condition instead assigns an independent fair coin flip to every response. For G G responses to one prompt, r 1 , … , r G ∼ iid Bernoulli ⁡ ( 1 / 2 ) , ( r 1 , … , r G ) ⟂ ( x , y ( 1 ) , … , y ( G ) ) r_{1},\ldots,r_{G}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{iid}}}{{\sim}}\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2),\qquad(r_{1},\ldots,r_{G})\perp(x,y^{(1)},\ldots,y^{(G)}) conditional on the preceding training history. sections.heading: 8 Extended Related Work
sections.text: The spurious-reward paradox connects two questions: where an improved answer comes from, and what the improvement tells us about the model. Work on contamination examines whether the answer was memorized; work on RL examines how training changes its probability. Probing raises the related question of whether a successful measurement reveals the model’s knowledge or supplies what was missing. We discuss these connections below.

sections.heading: 8.1 Data Contamination and Memorized Answers
sections.text: Wu et al. (2026) investigate whether gains under weak or incorrect rewards depend on benchmark contamination. They find evidence of contamination in Qwen2.5 and introduce RandomCalculation, a generator of fresh arithmetic problems. Correct rewards produce sustained gains on these problems in their experiments, whereas random and incorrect rewards do not. Their result shows why gains on familiar benchmarks require further examination: a model can become better at returning an answer without becoming better at solving a new problem. Yan et al. (2026) approach this question through a memorization circuit. Earlier work interprets feed-forward layers as key–value memories ( Geva et al., 2021 ) and uses interventions in middle-layer MLPs to study factual associations ( Meng et al., 2022 ) . Yan et al. combine partial-prompt evaluations, activation patching, and neuron interventions to argue that middle layers retrieve memorized answers while later layers adapt to the retrieved signal. They distinguish these results from smaller gains on LiveMathBench, which they tentatively attribute to format alignment or dormant capability. Their account thus concerns the source of particular benchmark gains. Related mechanistic work further separates whether information is stored by a model from whether it is successfully expressed in its output. Yu et al. (2024a) identify two distinct failure modes behind non-factual hallucinations: insufficient factual information in lower-layer MLPs and failures in upper-layer attention to select the appropriate factual attribute. Thus, the same incorrect behavior can arise from substantially different internal states. Hong et al. (2025b) find a related dissociation in machine unlearning: methods can suppress a concept behaviorally while leaving recoverable traces of the corresponding parametric knowledge. Hong et al. (2025a) further identify residual-stream features that distinguish reasoning from memory recall and show that intervening on these features can causally shift model performance between the two. Together, these results motivate distinguishing whether information has been stored, whether it is accessible to the computation being performed, and whether it is successfully used in the final response. Niu et al. (2025a) examine a related distinction in in-context learning using tasks built from random token sequences. Models can follow novel patterns, although performance remains sensitive to token frequency and task configuration. Their findings distinguish generalization beyond memorized instances from independence of pre-training statistics. In our view, remembering an answer and learning how to answer should be distinguished. A model that applies a familiar arithmetic procedure to a new problem is generalizing, even if it has seen many similar problems. Synthetic instances reduce the opportunity to retrieve a specific question–answer pair, though template generation alone cannot certify absence from a large training corpus. Prior exposure to the underlying skill is part of what we want to measure. The question is why further training can help one checkpoint use that skill more readily than another.

sections.heading: 8.2 RL Training and Pre-existing Capabilities
sections.text: Shao et al. (2026) show that format, incorrect, and random rewards can improve Qwen2.5-Math , with less consistent benefits across other model families. They propose that clipping in GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) creates asymmetric updates favoring behavior to which the model already assigns high probability. Their Appendix B.2 also reports occasional high-performing runs without clipping. This leaves room for clipping to affect stability without being necessary for every gain. The reward conditions themselves also differ: incorrect-answer rewards consult the verifier, format rewards inspect the response, and independent random rewards do neither. Chen et al. (2025) argue that clipping bias alone does not explain the gains. They relate clipping to entropy reduction and stability, but find that performance can improve with either increasing or decreasing entropy. Their reward-misalignment analysis compares random assignments with correctness-based assignments within a response group. A model that produces more correct responses has fewer incorrect trajectories available to reward by chance. This gives current task performance a direct role in explaining which models benefit. More broadly, the information and granularity supplied by the reward can substantially change the outcome of RL training. Cao et al. (2024) use LLM-generated critiques to turn sparse sequence-level feedback into token- or span-level intermediate rewards, improving learning efficiency and final performance across text-generation tasks. Their setting enriches the reward channel, whereas our random-reward intervention deliberately removes correctness information from it. Both make explicit that what further training can attain depends not only on the starting policy, but also on what information the adaptation procedure is allowed to provide. Our shared-rollout experiment asks about a further part of the process. Two learners receive identical responses and identical random rewards, so each pair has the same rewarded-incorrect and unrewarded-correct responses. We then compare how the learners change (Appendix 11.7 ). The experiment holds the training material fixed to examine the learner’s contribution. It does not contradict Chen et al.’s on-policy analysis, whose assumptions and object of study differ from this offline comparison. Related work asks whether correctness-guided RL mainly improves the use of capabilities acquired during pre-training. Yue et al. (2025) find that RL gains at small sampling budgets can coexist with broader problem coverage by the base model at large pass@ k k . Zhao et al. (2025) vary pre-training data and model scale, finding that post-training amplifies patterns established during pre-training. These results connect post-training behavior to the model’s history. They do not establish that a finite sampling budget recovers everything a model could learn to do, or that correct rewards supply no task information. At the parameter level, quantized LLM weights remain substantially compressible ( Mao et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . This redundancy is consistent with small updates changing which existing behaviors a model uses, although we do not test that connection. Clay et al. (2026) study the interaction between the starting model, reward, and training questions. Rewards for intermediate progress can enable learning where final-answer-only rewards fail. Under random rewards, mathematical prompts can produce different outcomes from broader prompt collections: Qwen2.5-Math improves under narrow mathematics training but shows little improvement on MATH and declines on AMC under WildChat prompts. They also observe different patterns of degradation under broad and mathematics-only training in OLMo-3. Their experiments retain meaningful questions, whereas our input controls also replace question content with random tokens. Prompting provides a related way to change task performance without updating model parameters. Jin et al. (2024) find that expanding the reasoning steps in chain-of-thought demonstrations can improve accuracy, while compressing them can reduce it. They also find that some arithmetic tasks are relatively insensitive to an incorrect intermediate step. Their illustrated error control retains the correct final answer, however, so an incorrect rationale is not equivalent to removing correctness information. These results highlight how the form of the input can affect performance, complementing our analysis of training inputs. Input tokens can shape predictions without carrying task content: Niu et al. (2025b) find that LLMs assign higher logits and probabilities to tokens that appear in the context, even when those tokens are sampled at random. Random-token inputs therefore remove the mathematical problem without making the prompt inert. The development of the starting model is also visible through in-context learning. Across Pythia checkpoints, Niu et al. (2025a) find that pattern following with frequent tokens develops earlier than with rare tokens, while tasks requiring integration of linguistic and factual information develop later and more gradually. Reachability probing complements this analysis by measuring how the response to further parameter updates changes across checkpoints. Complementary work traces changes in a model’s internal organization during training and across network depth. Tracking Pythia through its pre-training checkpoints, Lee et al. (2025) find that the relationship between linguistic compositionality and representation geometry develops as linguistic features are learned. At the layer level, Cheng et al. (2024) identify a high-dimensional representational phase associated with linguistic abstraction, transfer to downstream tasks, and language-modeling performance. Jin et al. (2026) find that last-hidden-state representations become sparser as task difficulty increases and, by pretraining small transformers from scratch, that representational density develops as a learned property of data familiarity. These studies do not measure reachability, but they provide complementary evidence that a model’s observable task performance need not fully characterize the internal state from which subsequent computation or learning proceeds. Taken together, these studies make the conditions of further training part of the question. Current accuracy describes the responses a model already produces; sampling examines what else it can produce without changing its parameters; adaptation examines what becomes attainable after updates. We use reachability for this last property, specifying the training procedure, available information, and budget. Random rewards remove correctness feedback from the reward channel while leaving the model and its training inputs able to affect what happens next.

sections.heading: 8.3 Probing, Information, and the Use of Knowledge
sections.text: Probes test what can be recovered from a model’s representations. Linear classifiers at intermediate layers measure their usefulness for prediction ( Alain and Bengio, 2017 ) ; diagnostic NLP tasks examine linguistic properties ( Conneau et al., 2018 ) ; structural probes recover syntactic distances and depths through a transformation of word representations ( Hewitt and Manning, 2019 ) . The interpretation depends on the representation, predictor, training data, and evaluation criterion ( Belinkov, 2022 ) . The evaluation criterion matters for behavioral assessments as well: Niu and Penn (2020) show that conclusions about language models’ grammatical knowledge depend on how model probabilities are scored against acceptability judgments, and argue for the point-biserial correlation. The predictor’s own learning creates an attribution problem. Hewitt and Liang (2019) introduce control tasks with random labels assigned to word types, measuring whether a probe can memorize a mapping unrelated to the linguistic property of interest. Their selectivity measure compares performance on the linguistic and control tasks. Voita and Titov (2020) instead use minimum description length to account for the model complexity or training data needed to obtain a good predictor. Both go beyond final probe accuracy when deciding what credit belongs to the representation. Niu et al. (2022a) address attribution through controlled comparisons of information sources. Their RH Probe combines BERT representations with part-of-speech tags and Roark–Hollingshead syntactic distances, then removes sources during training or perturbs them during evaluation. These experiments show that BERT contributes useful syntactic information while explicit syntactic encodings can still improve parsing. They also note that a parameter-free extraction algorithm can supply structural assumptions of its own. The preference for a simple probe is itself disputed. Pimentel et al. (2020) formulate probing as estimating mutual information between representations and annotations, for which a more expressive predictor can improve the estimate. Restricting the predictor may conceal information that is present but difficult to extract. Information content and ease of extraction are therefore different objects of study. Methods that order representation dimensions by importance, such as variational nested dropout ( Cui et al., 2021 ) , make a related point: how much of a representation is useful depends on how much of it the reader is allowed to use. Our use of training response concerns the latter distinction without requiring this debate to be resolved in favor of one probe architecture. Zhu and Rudzicz (2020) connect these accounts by decomposing probing cross-entropy into label entropy, representation–label mutual information, and the probe’s error in approximating the conditional label distribution. They also show that cross-entropy versions of selectivity and information gain have closely related estimation errors, with an equivalence under idealized randomization assumptions. Subsequent formulations make the reader of a representation explicit. Pimentel and Cotterell (2021) account for an agent’s background knowledge and finite data through Bayesian mutual information. Hewitt et al. (2021) , using 𝒱 \mathcal{V} -information ( Xu et al., 2019 ) , measure what a representation adds beyond a baseline for a specified predictive family. Both distinguish preserved information from information useful to a particular predictor. Zhu et al. (2022) connect these measurements to subsequent learning by predicting supervised fine-tuning performance from linguistic probing scores. For each of six GLUE classification tasks, three selected task–layer scores predict fine-tuning performance with lower error than random-feature baselines. Reachability asks a related question about the model’s own adaptation: what performance can further training attain under the allowed procedures and budget? Successful decoding also leaves open whether the model uses the decoded property. Ravichander et al. (2021) show that representations can encode properties unnecessary for the original task. Amnesic probing instead removes information associated with a property and measures the behavioral effect ( Elazar et al., 2021 ) . Tiblias et al. (2025) combine geometric analysis with intervention: temporal feature manifolds change with the task prompt, and perturbing their identified subspaces impairs reasoning. Comparisons with random subspaces help establish the functional relevance of the recovered structure. Recent work similarly combines representational readout with causal intervention. Ji et al. (2025) identify verbal uncertainty as a linear feature in LLM representations and show that manipulating the feature changes expressed uncertainty and can reduce confident hallucinations. Yu et al. (2024b) ; Shayegani et al. (2025) study a refusal feature in the residual stream, show that suppressing it reproduces a mechanism shared by adversarial jailbreaks, and use this mechanistic account to construct an efficient adversarial-training procedure. Yang et al. (2025) take a further step by amortizing an activation-steering intervention into model weights, so that a representational control signal discovered at inference time becomes a persistent behavioral change after training. These examples illustrate a progression from decoding a property, to establishing a functional role through intervention, to altering what a model reliably produces after adaptation. Reachability is complementary: rather than prespecifying an internal feature, it asks what task behavior training can make attainable from the checkpoint under specified information and optimization constraints. Similar care is needed when interpreting where knowledge resides: Tenney et al. (2019) interpret layerwise results as an NLP-like processing sequence, while Niu et al. (2022b) find that token position, probe training stage, and random seed complicate that account. Extending layerwise probing to LLMs, Jin et al. (2025) train linear classifiers on factual, emotional, and reasoning tasks and compare the depths at which probe performance improves or stabilizes. Their concept depth characterizes supervised readout across network layers, complementing our comparison of training responses across pre-training checkpoints. Niu et al. (2024) find that edits to factual associations often fail to generalize across inverse relations and synonymous expressions. Their results distinguish the ability to alter a token prediction from stronger claims about knowledge storage. Related ambiguity arises in circuit and sheaf discovery Yu et al. (2025) . Chen et al. (2026) hold model weights fixed and recover structurally distinct, low-overlap mechanisms that support the same task. Their results separate functional sufficiency from claims of a unique internal mechanism. A probe can recover real structure without establishing the larger explanation proposed for it. For generative models, Orgad et al. (2024) find internal information about correctness that is not always expressed in the generated answer. Tuned lenses decode intermediate states into vocabulary distributions ( Belrose et al., 2025 ) , and sparse autoencoders learn features from activations ( Bricken et al., 2023 ) . The predictive distribution itself can also be read out as a code length, as in learned lossless compressors for images and gigapixel pathology slides ( Mao et al., 2025a ; Mao et al., 2025d ) . These methods do not all use task labels, so the absence of label supervision alone does not distinguish our approach from every internal readout. Our measurement instead requires the model itself to perform the task after adaptation. Random rewards allow us to study this response without supplying correct-answer feedback during training. The resulting measurement still depends on the adaptation procedure, and does not establish that a complete successful procedure existed unchanged in the starting checkpoint.

sections.heading: From gradients to behavior.
sections.text: A zero-mean gradient need not leave expected behavior unchanged. For a smooth statistic f f , a second-order expansion under suitable regularity gives 𝔼 ⁡ [ f ⁡ ( θ + η ​ g ^ ) − f ⁡ ( θ ) ∣ θ ] = η 2 2 ​ tr ⁡ ( ∇ 2 f ​ ( θ ) ​ C ​ ( θ ) ) + o ⁡ ( η 2 ) , C ⁡ ( θ ) = Cov ⁡ ( g ^ ∣ θ ) . \mathbb{E}[f(\theta+\eta\widehat{g})-f(\theta)\mid\theta]=\frac{\eta^{2}}{2}\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\nabla^{2}f(\theta)C(\theta)\right)+o(\eta^{2}),\qquad C(\theta)=\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat{g}\mid\theta). sections.heading: 10 Experimental Setup
sections.text: We compare checkpoints under fixed training conditions, then vary the training inputs and the source of the responses to examine what contributes to the observed gains. This section gives the data, protocols, and evaluation rules. Appendix 11 reports the outcomes for every seed.

sections.heading: 10.1.1 OLMo-2 training checkpoints
sections.text: Our main model is OLMo-2-1124-7B . P1 denotes its first stage of pre-training, ending at 3,896B tokens; P2 denotes the ingredient-1 mid-training continuation. A label such as P2 +5B counts additional tokens after P1. The GSM scan includes 25 P1 and 12 P2 checkpoints. Code and lookup use eight P1 checkpoints, at 5B, 462B, 839B, 1,259B, 2,098B, 2,937B, 3,532B, and 3,896B, and four P2 checkpoints, at +5B, +13B, +26B, and +50B. The complete GSM coverage appears in Tables 8 and 9 . The additional OLMo-2 controls use the P1 endpoint, P2 +5B, and P2 +50B. The earlier exploratory study also includes P2 +21B. These checkpoints let us compare the end of pre-training with both the beginning and end of mid-training while keeping architecture and parameter count fixed.

sections.heading: 10.1.2 Synthetic arithmetic
sections.text: We generate 1,000 arithmetic word problems from templates and hold out 200 for evaluation. The split separates problem instances; training and evaluation can share template families. Each question follows the instruction Solve the math problem. Show your reasoning and put the final answer on a line like: #### <number>. The worked answer is not given as a target in random-reward training. Both training generation and greedy evaluation use a 96-token response cap. Numerical correctness uses an absolute tolerance of 10 − 6 10^{-6} . The primary, lenient extractor checks for a number following #### , an annotated equation, an answer phrase, and finally the last number in the response, in that order. A separate strict score requires a standalone #### <number> line. We report both because a correct answer can appear without the requested format. OLMo-2 mid-training includes GSM-style material from TinyGSM-MIND and the GSM8K training split, alongside changes in the broader data mixture and learning-rate schedule. The checkpoint comparison therefore includes changing task exposure. Generated evaluation problems reduce dependence on particular benchmark answers without excluding familiarity with the underlying procedures.

sections.heading: 10.1.3 Code generation
sections.text: The MBPP dataset ( Odena et al., 2021 ) used here contains 964 problems, with 764 for training and 200 for evaluation. Each prompt includes the first test: Write a Python function to solve the following problem. Only output the function definition, no explanation. Problem: <question> Your code should pass this test: <first test> Solution: Responses are capped at 256 tokens. The evaluator extracts the code, appends the test setup and tests, and executes it with a ten-second timeout. A problem is correct only if execution completes and all tests pass. Accuracy is the fraction of problems solved. The visible test supplies task information in both GT and Random conditions. Random rewards remove feedback about whether the generated program passed, while preserving the information already in its prompt.

sections.heading: 10.1.4 Compositional lookup
sections.text: We generate 1,000 problems using invented people and cities. Each problem contains eight people, four cities, and four pairs of people. Each pair contributes a relation and a city fact, giving eight facts presented in shuffled order. One-hop questions ask where a named person lives. Two-hop questions combine a relation with a location, for example A’s teacher is B and B lives in C , followed by Where does A’s teacher live? . The instruction is Answer the question using the facts. Put the final answer on a line like: #### <answer>. The generator alternates one- and two-hop questions. The fixed evaluation set contains 104 one-hop and 96 two-hop items, which are pooled in the main score. The checker compares the extracted answer with the correct city. Uniform choice among the four cities would give 25% accuracy, shown as a reference in Figure 8(b) ; it is not an assumption about the model’s actual starting policy.

sections.heading: 10.9 Statistical Analysis
sections.text: Training seeds are the units of replication. Comparisons pair shared seed IDs, keeping the earlier seed-dependent evaluation splits separate from the fixed-split scan. For P1/P2 comparisons, we first average over checkpoints within each phase and seed, then compare the seed-level averages. This accounts for seed reuse and limits the interpretation to the checkpoint grid studied. For paired score differences d s d_{s} , we use a two-sided permutation test with statistic | ∑ s d s | |\sum_{s}d_{s}| , enumerating sign assignments. It requires exchangeability within pairs, or independent paired differences symmetric about zero; equality of means alone is insufficient. Small samples are enumerated directly, and 32-seed comparisons use exact subset-sum counting on the 200-question score grid. Binary comparisons use exact McNemar tests on discordant pairs. Within a condition, a two-sided sign test instead asks whether nonzero changes are equally likely to be positive and negative. Ties remain in the reported counts but are omitted from that test. Success-rate intervals are marginal, two-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson intervals. They condition on the checkpoint, evaluation set, and protocol. With zero successes in eight runs, the upper endpoint is 1 − 0.025 1 / 8 ≈ 0.369 1-0.025^{1/8}\approx 0.369 ; eight failures leave considerable uncertainty about the population rate. Pooling outcomes across checkpoints does not turn them into draws from one common success probability, and the 200 evaluation questions do not provide 200 independent training seeds. We apply Holm correction within seven families: D/E comparisons (15 tests), other OLMo-2 input pairs (18), developmental contrasts (12), additional-model checkpoint and protocol contrasts (32), earlier controls (10), within-condition directional tests (150), and scan GT/Random comparisons (53). We also report a correction over all 290 evaluable tests. These analyses were chosen after inspecting results; correction accounts for the listed tests, not all prior protocol and hypothesis choices. The shared-rollout experiment has a separate family of six tests specified before its formal runs (Appendix 11.7 ).

sections.text: The checkpoint scans, input controls, and shared-rollout comparison comprise 932 distinct training runs. sections.heading: 11.1 OLMo-2 Checkpoint Development
sections.text: Tables 8 and 9 give all 444 GSM terminal scores. None of the 200 P1 Random runs ends at or above 50%, compared with 15 of 96 P2 runs. Within P2, however, 35 runs reach this threshold at a scheduled evaluation. Mid-training therefore changes the range of outcomes observed under Random, while many improvements remain transient. The maxima also fluctuate across P2 checkpoints. Current greedy accuracy does not fully describe this development. The 462B and 839B checkpoints both score 3.5% before training, yet their best GT outcomes are 8.5% and 55.0%. The later checkpoint is a more useful starting point for this training procedure even though the frozen score is unchanged. We take this as evidence that changes relevant to post-training can precede their expression in the model’s greedy answers. This comparison matches the greedy scores, rather than the full initial response distributions.

sections.heading: Code generation becomes more responsive in mid-training.
sections.text: Most P1 code runs remain near zero. Random never exceeds 1.5%, and GT remains at or below 0.5% except at 2,098B, where it reaches 11.0%. All 16 P2 GT runs instead score at least 16.5%, with checkpoint maxima between 22.0% and 27.0%. The contrast persists across the P2 GT runs, rather than arising solely from taking a maximum over more seeds. Random produces gains less consistently. Its P2 maxima are 19.0%, 14.5%, 1.0%, and 19.0% at +5B, +13B, +26B, and +50B. At +13B and +50B, frozen greedy accuracy is zero, yet both GT and Random reach test-passing performance. A model that fails under greedy decoding can therefore still improve through adaptation. The weak +26B result and failed seeds also show that this response does not increase monotonically with training tokens.

Random remains weaker at this point, reaching at most 26.0%, close to the uniform-city reference. sections.heading: 11.4 The Developmental Pattern under Supervised Fine-Tuning
sections.text: Figure 6 (b) compares full-answer SFT with form-only (number-masked) SFT. Full-answer SFT trains on the worked answer. Form-only SFT masks numbers in both questions and solutions while retaining the wording and solution structure. The latter still supplies information about how to approach the task, although it withholds the numerical content of the answer. The ordering resembles the RL results: checkpoints become responsive to fuller supervision before the restricted form becomes effective. Since SFT uses neither policy-ratio clipping nor group-relative advantages, this parallel suggests a developmental explanation beyond those RL-specific mechanisms. The SFT comparison is qualitative. We recover 22 checkpoint values from the original figure’s vector paths; per-seed SFT results are unavailable. That figure reports best SFT scores, whereas the RL curves use best terminal scores, and the budgets, checkpoint coverage, selection rules, and evaluation details have not been established as matched. The comparison supports examining the order of developmental changes, rather than numerical equivalence between the two training procedures.

sections.heading: A correct answer need not follow the requested format.
sections.text: The highest MMLU-trained run has 86.5% lenient accuracy but zero strict accuracy and no #### markers. For example, Question: Victor buys 3 pages at $8 each and pays $84. How much change does Victor get? Model output: Victor pays 3 * 8 = $24 for the pages. Victor gets 84 - 24 = $60 in change. The response supplies the correct answer without the prescribed marker. The two high-scoring D runs likewise have quite different format rates, 89.0% and 14.5%. Numerical correctness and compliance with the answer format need to be examined separately. The conditions also differ in deterioration. Original GSM has three terminal gains above ten points and 15 collapses to at most 5% out of 32 runs; D has four gains and eight collapses. MMLU has two gains and one collapse out of 16, and shuffled GSM has two gains and six collapses. These samples do not establish an ordering of input quality. They show that the same random-reward procedure can produce different distributions of outcomes depending on what the model trains on. The clearest D/E statistical contrast concerns the magnitude of change. Sixteen of 32 D runs change by more than ten points in either direction, compared with none in E (exact McNemar p = 3.05 × 10 − 5 p=3.05\times 10^{-5} ; Holm p H = 4.27 × 10 − 4 p_{H}=4.27\times 10^{-4} ). Positive gains alone, four versus zero, give p p = 0.125. The evidence for greater responsiveness is therefore stronger than the evidence for a higher success probability. Since D and E also differ in token construction (Appendix 10.3 ), this supports a task-cue interpretation without isolating the effect of the instruction alone.

sections.heading: 11.7 Shared-Rollout Cross-Training
sections.text: This experiment separates the model that produces training responses from the model updated on them. We use the final P1 checkpoint of OLMo-2 and its first released P2 checkpoint, +5B. Each is both a frozen response source and a learner, giving four source–learner combinations. Sixteen replicate blocks, 51001–51016, contain all four combinations, for 64 runs of 500 updates. The main outcomes appear in Table 1 .

sections.heading: Shared training material.
sections.text: The two checkpoints share the same tokenizer and configuration, so responses can be passed directly as token IDs. We use the scan’s 800/200 GSM split and the first 500 questions of the ordered training set, visiting one per step. Each frozen source samples four responses per question with the math template, temperature 1, top- p p = 0.95, and a 96-token cap, in batches of ten prompts. No response is filtered, resampled, or sorted by correctness. The 32 source streams contain 64,000 responses. Within a replicate, all four learners share a 500 × 4 500\times 4 table of independent Bernoulli ( 1 / 2 ) (1/2) rewards and the same initial LoRA tensors. Within each source condition, the two learners also share all response tokens and loss masks. Advantages use the population standard deviation with 10 − 6 10^{-6} stabilization, and constant-reward groups have zero advantage. Correctness is used only for evaluation and diagnostics.

sections.heading: Offline updates.

These are off-policy random-advantage updates; they do not estimate the on-policy GRPO gradient without bias. The base weights remain frozen. LoRA uses rank 8, scaling 16, and zero dropout on attention query, key, value, and output projections and MLP gate, up, and down projections. Unlike the on-policy Random runs, these runs have neither the reference coefficient 0.01 nor weight decay 0.01, so even matching source and learner does not replicate the on-policy condition. sections.text: For the P2 learner, P2 responses yield six improved runs and no terminal scores at or below 5%, while P1 responses yield three improved runs and six such low endpoints. Both improved P1 runs use P2 responses. An exploratory interaction gives a +6.84-point mean change in the learner gap across sources, with 13 positive and three negative block differences (sign-test p p = 0.0213). Exploratory source tests give p p = 0.3018 for P1 learners and p p = 0.0768 for P2 learners. These tests were outside the planned six-test family. We do not compare the learners’ collapse rates at the 5% cutoff because P1 already starts below it. There are two prevailing explanations for the surprising finding that even random rewards can improve the performance of large language models (LLMs): one attributes the gains to particular mechanisms within RL training ( Shao et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) ; the other to data contamination ( Yan et al., 2026 ) . Our results motivate a different view: spurious-reward RL can probe a model’s reachability, or what further training can attain from its current state under specified constraints, beyond what is reflected in its current performance. Two OLMo checkpoints with the same accuracy on synthetic arithmetic (3.5%), for example, reach 8.5% and 55% in their best runs under the same correctness-rewarded RL. Examining OLMo checkpoints across pre-training and mid-training reveals three distinct regimes of training response: early on, RL produces little improvement even when correct answers are rewarded; later in pre-training, rewarding correct answers becomes effective while random rewards remain weak; and, upon entering mid-training, even random rewards can produce large gains. A similar ordering appears in a number-masked supervised fine-tuning (SFT) analysis of these checkpoints, suggesting that the pattern is not specific to a particular RL mechanism. Moreover, RL with random rewards offers a distinctive perspective on what training can make an LLM do, since its reward signal supplies no information about which answers are correct. By asking what training can attain without correctness feedback, it addresses the label-leakage side of a central problem in decodability-based probing: whether a successful probe reveals the model’s capabilities or learns the task itself. \metadatafont Date: September 2026 Code: https://github.com/mynotwo/rl-random-prob 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has played a central role in improving the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and ushering in an “age of LLM agents.” A natural intuition is that LLMs can learn from reward signals by favoring better responses over worse ones. Yet Shao et al. (2026) recently reported that even spurious (random) rewards can improve model performance. Why can a model improve when its rewards are assigned at random, providing no more correctness information than a random coin toss? This counterintuitive finding prompted a number of investigations and led Yan et al. (2026) to coin the term spurious-reward paradox . Explaining it requires understanding what shapes the model’s response to training beyond correctness feedback. There are currently two main lines of explanation for the paradox, but neither provides a complete account in light of our new empirical results. The first attributes the gains to data contamination ( Yan et al., 2026 ) . The gains we observe on synthetically generated problems suggest, however, that the phenomenon cannot be attributed entirely to data leakage. The second looks to particular mechanisms within RL training. Shao et al. (2026) conjecture that clipping in GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) favors behavior to which the model already assigns high probability. Chen et al. (2025) , however, argue that clipping bias does not explain the gains. They explain the paradox through the model’s current performance, as reflected in its rollouts: more accurate models generate fewer incorrect responses that can be rewarded by chance. Nevertheless, when two checkpoints are trained offline on the same rollouts with the same random rewards, the later, higher-accuracy checkpoint shows larger mean gains under both rollout sources. This suggests that understanding the gains requires looking beyond the model’s current performance to properties of the learner that shape its response to the same training signal. In particular, capabilities the model already has but does not fully put to use, or its dormant capability , may play an important role. We instead consider the model’s dormant capability together with the information provided in the question prompt. A model may not yet reliably generate the correct answer, yet the prompt can still elicit behavior that training can act on. Under random rewards, some useful responses may be reinforced by chance; which behaviors can be elicited and reinforced should therefore depend in part on the starting model and the information in the input. On this account, training can improve performance even when the reward does not tell the model which answers are correct. We can therefore use a model’s response to random-reward RL training as a probe. We introduce reachability to describe how far, and how readily, a model can improve from its current state under specified constraints on the training procedure, the information supplied, and the training budget. Specifically, we use random-reward reachability to probe dormant capability. We prove that, under random-reward RL training, the reward channel carries no correctness information, allowing us to study what training can attain without correctness feedback. This isolates the label-leakage side of a longstanding question in probing: whether a successful probe reveals the model’s dormant capability or learns the task from its own supervision ( Hewitt and Liang, 2019 ) . Applying random-reward probing in the wild across OLMo checkpoints reveals three stages of LLM capability development. Early in pre-training, OLMo-2-1124-7B is dormant : even RL with ground-truth (GT) rewards yields little improvement. As pre-training progresses, the model becomes receptive : GT rewards become effective, suggesting that the model has acquired the basic task knowledge needed to benefit from further training. Random rewards remain weak, however, suggesting that the model has acquired relevant knowledge and skills but has yet to integrate them into capabilities it can readily draw on. When the model enters mid-training, it becomes autodidactic : training can now help it put this knowledge to use even without a reward signal that tells it which answers are correct. These results suggest that a model’s receptiveness to post-training depends on its overall capability at that point in training, and that reachability provides a viable way to study it. Contributions We make three contributions: (1) we provide an alternative account of the spurious-reward paradox that incorporates the starting model and the information in the input (§ 3 ); (2) we formalize reachability as a framework for probing what further training can attain and develop random-reward RL as a correctness-free probe (§ 4 ); and (3) we identify a three-stage pattern in training response that reveals changes not fully reflected in current task performance (§ 5 ). 2 Background, Related Work, and Experimental Setup Before discussing our experiments and results, we review RL, the spurious-reward paradox, and its two prevailing accounts and their limitations. We then revisit the probing debate: whether a probe reveals the model’s knowledge or learns the task itself. 1 1 1 For the sake of space, we defer a more comprehensive literature review to Appendix 8 . Reinforcement Learning with Spurious Rewards In a typical RLVR setting 2 2 2 Appendix 7 reviews core RL concepts and notation, following Shao et al. (2026) and Chen et al. (2025) . , the model generates a response, and a verifier assigns a reward by checking the answer or executing tests. Methods such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) can train models without worked solutions by sampling multiple responses to the same prompt and updating the model based on their relative rewards. Surprisingly, Shao et al. (2026) found that even spurious rewards —rewards with little, no, or even negative correlation with answer correctness—can elicit strong reasoning performance under certain conditions. Subsequent work has proposed several explanations for this phenomenon, including reduced reward-misalignment damage in more accurate models ( Chen et al., 2025 ) and increased model confidence through entropy minimization ( Agarwal et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) . In this work, we study spurious rewards from a different perspective. We show that random rewards—a special case of spurious rewards with zero correlation with correctness—can serve as an effective probe of dormant LLM capabilities in generation tasks such as reasoning and coding. The Probing Debate: Measuring an LLM’s Dormant Capability Probing has long been a central tool for studying what models know and what they are capable of. The usual recipe is straightforward: freeze the model, extract its representations, and train a classifier, or probe , to predict a property of interest. Good probing performance is then taken as evidence that the model has learned something about that property. But whose knowledge have we found? The probe has, after all, been given the answers during training. As Hewitt and Liang (2019) ask, “can we conclude that the representation encodes linguistic structure, or has the probe just learned the task?” This question has motivated different accounts of decodability : what can be recovered from a representation, and under what conditions. Pimentel et al. (2020) formulate probing as estimating mutual information between representations and task labels. But information can be preserved without being easy to extract. The Bayesian account of Pimentel and Cotterell (2021) considers what a learner can extract given its prior knowledge and finite training data. Predictive 𝒱 \mathcal{V} -information makes the predictor family explicit ( Xu et al., 2019 ) , while conditional probing asks what the representation contributes beyond a baseline ( Hewitt et al., 2021 ) . The question thus becomes not merely whether information is present, but under what conditions it can be used. Nevertheless, probes for LLM capabilities still largely rely on supervised learning from task labels and therefore do not remove the concern raised by Hewitt and Liang (2019) : the probe may learn the task from its own supervision. We show that random-reward RL can probe what training can attain while excluding correctness information from the reward signal, thereby isolating this label-leakage component of the broader probing problem. While this debate may seem to have gone quiet, its central questions have only become more relevant and important, resurfacing under different names. Recent work such as sparse autoencoders (SAE; Bricken et al., 2023 , inter alia ) , the linear representation hypothesis ( Park et al., 2023 ; Lampinen et al., 2026 , inter alia ) , and the J-space ( Gurnee et al., 2026 ) again raises the question of what the structures recovered from a model’s representations tell us about what the model knows and can do. 3 Explaining the Spurious-Reward Paradox: Learner and Input We now examine why LLMs can improve under random-reward RL. Previous accounts ( Shao et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) do not account for two observations we present below: different learner checkpoints respond differently to identical rollouts and rewards, and the same checkpoint responds differently across the two random-token input conditions. These results point to the starting model and the information in the input as additional determinants of training response. Our main experiments follow the publicly released checkpoints of OLMo-2-1124-7B ( OLMo et al., 2025 ) through pre-training (P1) and mid-training (P2). P1 uses a broad corpus dominated by web data, while P2 introduces a curated mixture of high-quality and task-focused data. The checkpoints span both stages, with architecture and parameter count held fixed. We generate rollouts from each frozen checkpoint and train both learners on each set, giving four source–learner combinations. Within each source, both learners receive exactly the same cached rollouts and random rewards and start from identical LoRA weights. We run 16 paired replicates for 500 updates each. The rollouts remain fixed throughout training, so differences between the learners cannot be attributed to differences in the responses or rewards they receive. (2025) explain the spurious-reward paradox through the model’s current performance and rollout quality, arguing that training stronger models “incurs less total misalignment damage … and is therefore more likely to yield improvements under random rewards.” That mechanism cannot by itself explain the learner difference here: within each source condition, P1 and P2 receive the same responses and the same random rewards, so the number and identity of accidentally rewarded responses are fixed. Their account may still explain variation across rollout sources, but the contrast between learners requires an additional property of the learner itself. Reachability and an Account of the Spurious-Reward Paradox Taken together, these findings motivate an account of the spurious-reward paradox in terms of the starting model, the information in the input, and the model’s reachability , which we formalize in the next section. In short, the reward function determines how sampled answers are reinforced or suppressed, but the effect of those updates also depends on the starting model and the input. Even when rewards are assigned by random coin tosses and contain no correctness information, the prompt can still elicit useful behavior, and some random updates can reinforce it. If the starting model can already produce task-relevant behavior from the information in the input, some random-reward trajectories may therefore make that behavior more usable and improve task performance. The two experiments examine two factors not captured by rollout quality alone. First, P2 changes more than P1 when trained on identical rollouts and random rewards, showing that the learner state matters. In the second, the two random-token input conditions produce sharply different outcomes. The retained instruction and template markers still specify the task domain, request a reasoning chain, define the final-answer format, and structure the prompt. They do not supply the missing mathematical problem or its answer, but they provide task information that the model can draw on. This gives a different view of dormant capability: random-reward training lets us ask how much task performance further training can attain from a model without correctness feedback through the reward. We call this property reachability . 4 Reachability Probing with Random-Reward RL This new way of studying a model’s capability offers a general-purpose approach to probing that provides no correctness feedback during adaptation. It thus directly addresses the longstanding question of whether a probe reveals the model’s capability or learns the task from its own supervision. This probe also yields new findings about the development of models’ dormant capability, which are particularly relevant today, when post-training plays an ever more important role in developing LLM capabilities. In this section, we provide a formal definition of our reachability probe. We first discuss what information means when studying a model’s dormant capability, and then formalize reachability. We next present a short proof that random reward signals do not introduce correctness information through the reward channel. Finally, we introduce random-reward RL as a reachability probe, which we use in the next section on real LLMs. What Do We Mean by Information and Dormant Capability? We believe we have taken a step forward toward a better understanding of LLMs and how their capabilities develop; nevertheless, more questions arise as we edge toward the truth. Our theoretical account and empirical results suggest that there is usable information in input questions that LLMs can use even without correctness feedback from rewards. Nevertheless, studying the exact mechanism by which this information is utilized is a natural extension of this work. It could be a sign that, after a period of training, LLMs begin to bring their knowledge and skills together and show early signs of self-improvement: telling the model what task to attempt may be enough for it to improve through further training. The mechanism could also be superficial. The model may simply learn a better decoding strategy that generates correct responses more reliably. While shallow, such a strategy is certainly a capability; it does not, however, by itself establish the consistency across equivalent expressions that we would expect of “knowledge” ( Niu et al., 2024 ) . Future work can build on these findings by studying how random-reward training affects pass@ k k across sampling budgets ( Yue et al., 2025 ) and the consistency of responses across equivalent questions. Moreover, to keep this paper within a reasonable scope, we focus on RL as the vehicle for reachability-based probing. Yet other modes of post-training can also be used to develop a whole suite of reachability probes that help us better understand LLMs. References Agarwal et al.
