Work on contamination examines whether the answer was memorized; work on RL examines how training changes its probability. Probing raises the related question of whether a successful measurement reveals the model’s knowledge or supplies what was missing. We discuss these connections below. 8.1 Data Contamination and Memorized Answers Wu et al. (2026) investigate whether gains under weak or incorrect rewards depend on benchmark contamination. They find evidence of contamination in Qwen2.5 and introduce RandomCalculation, a generator of fresh arithmetic problems. Correct rewards produce sustained gains on these problems in their experiments, whereas random and incorrect rewards do not. Their result shows why gains on familiar benchmarks require further examination: a model can become better at returning an answer without becoming better at solving a new problem. Yan et al. (2026) approach this question through a memorization circuit. Earlier work interprets feed-forward layers as key–value memories ( Geva et al., 2021 ) and uses interventions in middle-layer MLPs to study factual associations ( Meng et al., 2022 ) . Yan et al. combine partial-prompt evaluations, activation patching, and neuron interventions to argue that middle layers retrieve memorized answers while later layers adapt to the retrieved signal. They distinguish these results from smaller gains on LiveMathBench, which they tentatively attribute to format alignment or dormant capability. Their account thus concerns the source of particular benchmark gains. Related mechanistic work further separates whether information is stored by a model from whether it is successfully expressed in its output. Yu et al. (2024a) identify two distinct failure modes behind non-factual hallucinations: insufficient factual information in lower-layer MLPs and failures in upper-layer attention to select the appropriate factual attribute. Thus, the same incorrect behavior can arise from substantially different internal states. Hong et al. (2025b) find a related dissociation in machine unlearning: methods can suppress a concept behaviorally while leaving recoverable traces of the corresponding parametric knowledge. Hong et al. (2025a) further identify residual-stream features that distinguish reasoning from memory recall and show that intervening on these features can causally shift model performance between the two. Together, these results motivate distinguishing whether information has been stored, whether it is accessible to the computation being performed, and whether it is successfully used in the final response. Niu et al. (2025a) examine a related distinction in in-context learning using tasks built from random token sequences. Models can follow novel patterns, although performance remains sensitive to token frequency and task configuration. Their findings distinguish generalization beyond memorized instances from independence of pre-training statistics. In our view, remembering an answer and learning how to answer should be distinguished. A model that applies a familiar arithmetic procedure to a new problem is generalizing, even if it has seen many similar problems. Synthetic instances reduce the opportunity to retrieve a specific question–answer pair, though template generation alone cannot certify absence from a large training corpus. Prior exposure to the underlying skill is part of what we want to measure. The question is why further training can help one checkpoint use that skill more readily than another. 8.2 RL Training and Pre-existing Capabilities Shao et al. (2026) show that format, incorrect, and random rewards can improve Qwen2.5-Math , with less consistent benefits across other model families. They propose that clipping in GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) creates asymmetric updates favoring behavior to which the model already assigns high probability. Their Appendix B.2 also reports occasional high-performing runs without clipping. This leaves room for clipping to affect stability without being necessary for every gain. The reward conditions themselves also differ: incorrect-answer rewards consult the verifier, format rewards inspect the response, and independent random rewards do neither. Chen et al. (2025) argue that clipping bias alone does not explain the gains. They relate clipping to entropy reduction and stability, but find that performance can improve with either increasing or decreasing entropy. Their reward-misalignment analysis compares random assignments with correctness-based assignments within a response group. A model that produces more correct responses has fewer incorrect trajectories available to reward by chance. This gives current task performance a direct role in explaining which models benefit. (2024) use LLM-generated critiques to turn sparse sequence-level feedback into token- or span-level intermediate rewards, improving learning efficiency and final performance across text-generation tasks.
